The Biggest Risk Is Human

After $6.3 billion in crypto was stolen from Binance, the conversation quickly and understandably turned to how investors hold scarce assets such as gold and, especially, crypto. Where does the fund store its physical gold? How is its bitcoin secured?

Fair questions. But to understand what the Binance theft tells us about custody, it helps to look at how the attackers got in.

According to Binance’s preliminary investigation, one of its engineers applied for what looked like a real job. The company was fictitious. The coding assignment contained malware. That was one step in a months-long attack that ultimately drained internet-connected wallets at the exchange.

That fake hiring process is a textbook example of social engineering. The attackers used a believable job opportunity, hence human gullibility, to get an engineer to run malicious code.

Today, Nvidia announced an independent investigation into whether foreign intelligence targeted its CEO, Jensen Huang.

Huang acknowledged an affair. Several media outlets reported that U.S. officials believed the woman involved was a Chinese intelligence asset. China denies the allegation. Nvidia’s board said it had no reason at that point to believe company secrets had been compromised.

The Nvidia investigation is still open, but the allegations put the Binance story in a broader context. A job interview can get someone to run a piece of code. A relationship can give someone access to a person with sensitive information. What happens from there depends on what that person can access, share, or authorize.

In traditional finance, we see examples all the time. In 2024, 26 financial firms agreed to pay nearly $393 million in SEC penalties for failing to preserve electronic communications. That was a serious control failure. How many investors read those headlines and asked whether their stocks and bonds were properly held in custody?

The same distinction matters when we talk about bitcoin in cold storage or physical gold in a Swiss vault. Where and how the assets are held shapes what an attacker can reach. Who can authorize a transfer or release, and how that instruction is verified, shapes what they can move.

Both deserve continuous scrutiny. Review who has access. Test how transfer instructions are verified. Check what happens when someone tries to bypass a control. That work is especially important in bitcoin custody, where the technology and the ways attackers exploit it keep changing.

Yet, even the best technology depends on the judgment of the people who use it. A convincing recruiter or a familiar voice can get us to make a mistake the technology was never designed to catch.

The P in JEPA stands for predictive.
The main distinction is not between JEA and JEPA, but between Joint Embedding (predictive or not) and generative architectures.
Whether a predictor is necessary depends on the task.

Given observations x and y (y being available only during training), a generative architectures predicts y from x. The loss is the divergence between y and its prediction:
  L = divergence(y, pred(enc(x)) )

A JEA encodes y as well and minimizes the divergence between the representations of x and y, while preventing collapse:
  L = divergence( enc(y), enc(x) ) + R( enc(y), enc(x) )
Where R is the anti-collapse regularizer, which may be computed over a batch of samples.
JEA are used when the prediction has no particular direction, i.e. when x and y are different views of the same scene. The idea for JEA is very old. Becker and Hinton proposed a simple model in 1989 where the anticollapse was based on information maximization. Schmidhuber had a version in 1992 based on redundancy minimization. At NIPS 1993, I proposed Siamese nets, which was a contrastive method to train JEA. Such contrastive methods gained popu.arity after Google's SimCLR paper in 2020. In 2021, Stéphane Deny in my group proposed the Barlow Twins redundancy reduction regularizer, which seemed to work at scale. This was shortly followed by VICReg by Adrien Bardes, Jean Ponce, and me, and last year by SIGReg by Randall Balestriero and me. 
DINO is a JEA method that comes from a long string of papers from Piotr Bojanowski's group at FAIR-Paris, starting with Noise as Targets (2017), Deep Clustering (2018-2020), and DINO v1-v3 which are contrastive between clusters, not samples.

JEPA adds a predictor, which is useful when the prediction is non-symetric. For example, when x is a degraded/corrupted version of y, or when x is a present observation and y a future observation (temporal prediction). The loss is:
  L = divergence( enc(y), pred(enc(x)) ) + R( enc(y), enc(x) )

All of these models can be augmented by an action variable a, fed to the predictor, encoding an action, intervention, or transformation to produce y from x.
This turns the system into a "world model". In a JEPA, the loss becomes
  L = divergence( enc(y), pred(enc(x), a) ) + R( enc(y), enc(x) )

What would Medicare for All look like if it were funded through a payroll tax?

CBO’s broadest illustrative coverage scenario requires approximately $3 trillion in additional annual federal funding in 2030, including dental, vision, hearing, and expanded long term care.

On an assumed $14 trillion payroll base, funding that gap would require approximately 21.4% in additional combined employer and employee payroll taxes, while existing federal health funding continues.

Split equally, with no cap on taxable wages, that means 10.7% from you and 10.7% from your employer:

• $100,000 salary: $10,700 more from each.

Everyone with taxable wages contributes, while coverage extends to children, retirees, and people who aren’t working.

Covered insurance premiums would disappear. Some workers and employers would save overall. Others would pay more. Employer contributions also affect the cost of employing someone and can influence wages and hiring.

This is an illustrative calculation using CBO’s spending estimate, not a CBO-scored tax proposal. Exemptions, changes in wages and employment, and other funding sources would change the required rate.
